subject: chemistry_2
question_text: Between C and CO, which is better reducing agent at 673 K?

verification.note: Unit 6 (Metallurgy) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.79-82, which prints the question and a model answer. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK CHECKED AND CORRECT (book p.79, VSAQ 5): the printed crossing temperature of 983 K was verified against standard thermodynamic data. For 2C + O₂ → 2CO, ΔG° ≈ −221 kJ − 0.179 T kJ; for 2CO + O₂ → 2CO₂, ΔG° ≈ −566 kJ + 0.173 T kJ. The two are equal at T ≈ 980 K, so 983 K is sound and the book's conclusion (CO better below it, C better above it) is right. BOOK TYPOS: the printed answer reads "intersed each other at 983K above" for "intersect each other at 983 K; above"; the sense is clear and the corrected wording is used on the card.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The answer
lines: CO is the better reducing agent at 673 K.
On the Ellingham diagram the line for
C → CO and the line for CO → CO₂ cross
673 K is below this crossing temperature.
steps.why: The question is answered entirely by where 673 K lies relative to the crossing point of the two carbon lines. Below 983 K the CO → CO₂ line lies lower, so CO has the more negative ΔG° per mole of oxygen and is the better reducing agent.
common_mistakes: Answering carbon out of habit. Carbon is the better reducing agent only above 983 K.
Comparing the two without the diagram. The answer changes with temperature, so the crossing point has to be quoted.
steps.memory_tip: 983 K is the dividing line. 673 K is below it, so the answer is CO.
steps.margin_note: Write the crossing temperature 983 K. The comparison cannot be marked without it.

steps.label: The Ellingham reason

lines.text: Below 983 K: CO.  Above 983 K: C.

lines: has the more negative ΔG°, so CO removes
oxygen more readily than carbon does.
lies lower and carbon is then better.
steps.why: The C → CO line falls as the temperature rises because one mole of O₂ makes two moles of gas, and the CO → CO₂ line rises because three moles of gas become two. The two lines therefore cross, and the crossing at about 983 K is the temperature at which the better reducing agent changes over.
common_mistakes: Saying carbon is always the better reducing agent. It is better only above the crossing temperature.
Writing 2CO + O₂ → CO₂. Two CO₂ are needed on the right for the carbon and the oxygen to balance.
steps.memory_tip: The carbon line falls, the CO line rises, and they cross at 983 K.
steps.margin_note: Both lines and the crossing temperature earn this mark. A small sketch of the crossing helps, but the words are enough.

insider_note: Learn the crossing temperature once and the whole Ellingham comparison follows: 983 K is the changeover, CO is the better reducing agent below it and carbon above it. Any temperature given in the question is answered by which side of 983 K it falls on.
